entries.7aa2a20fa6e682e25cffd410d652b1bd8ee025e8: <div sID="gen18858" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="23" osisID="Ezek.23" sID="Ezek.23"/> <div eID="gen18858" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18859" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen18860" type="x-p"/> This long chapter (as before <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.1-Ezek.16.62">ch. xvi.</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.1-Ezek.20.44">xx.</reference>) is a history of the apostasies of God's people from him and the aggravations of those apostasies under the similitude of corporal whoredom and adultery. Here the kingdoms of Israel and Judah, the ten tribes and the two, with their capital cities, Samaria and Jerusalem, are considered distinctly. Here is, I. The apostasy of Israel and Samaria from God (<reference osisRef="Ezek.23.1-Ezek.23.8">ver. 1-8</reference>) and their ruin for it, <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.9-Ezek.23.10">ver. 9, 10</reference>. II. The apostasy of Judah and Jerusalem from God (<reference osisRef="Ezek.23.11-Ezek.23.21">ver. 11-21</reference>) and sentence passed upon them, that they shall in like manner be destroyed for it, <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.22-Ezek.23.35">ver. 22-35</reference>. III. The joint wickedness of them both together (<reference osisRef="Ezek.23.36-Ezek.23.44">ver. 36-44</reference>) and the joint ruin of them both, <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.45-Ezek.23.49">ver. 45-49</reference>. And all that is written for warning against the sins of idolatry, and confidence in an arm of flesh, and sinful leagues and confederacies with wicked people (which are the sins here meant by committing whoredom), is that others may hear and fear, and not sin after the similitude of the transgressions of Israel and Judah.
entries.609edc06937fe53ae32e23587b63505bcc7551a4: <div eID="gen18860" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen18859" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Sins of Samaria and Jerusalem. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 591.)</title> <div sID="gen18861" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> The word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> came again unto me, saying, <hi type="super">2</hi> Son of man, there were two women, the daughters of one mother: <hi type="super">3</hi> And they committed whoredoms in Egypt; they committed whoredoms in their youth: there were their breasts pressed, and there they bruised the teats of their virginity. <hi type="super">4</hi> And the names of them <hi type="italic">were</hi> Aholah the elder, and Aholibah her sister: and they were mine, and they bare sons and daughters. Thus <hi type="italic">were</hi> their names; Samaria <hi type="italic">is</hi> Aholah, and Jerusalem Aholibah. <hi type="super">5</hi> And Aholah played the harlot when she was mine; and she doted on her lovers, on the Assyrians <hi type="italic">her</hi> neighbours, <hi type="super">6</hi> <hi type="italic">Which were</hi> clothed with blue, captains and rulers, all of them desirable young men, horsemen riding upon horses. <hi type="super">7</hi> Thus she committed her whoredoms with them, with all them <hi type="italic">that were</hi> the chosen men of Assyria, and with all on whom she doted: with all their idols she defiled herself. <hi type="super">8</hi> Neither left she her whoredoms <hi type="italic">brought</hi> from Egypt: for in her youth they lay with her, and they bruised the breasts of her virginity, and poured their whoredom upon her. <hi type="super">9</hi> Wherefore I have delivered her into the hand of her lovers, into the hand of the Assyrians, upon whom she doted. <hi type="super">10</hi> These discovered her nakedness: they took her sons and her daughters, and slew her with the sword: and she became famous among women; for they had executed judgment upon her. <div eID="gen18861" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18862" type="x-p"/> God had often spoken to Ezekiel, and by him to the people, to this effect, but now his word <hi type="italic">comes again;</hi> for <hi type="italic">God speaks</hi> the same thing <hi type="italic">once, yea, twice,</hi> yea, many a time, and all little enough, and too little, for <hi type="italic">man perceives it not.</hi> Note, To convince sinners of the evil of sin, and of their misery and danger by reason of it, there is need of <hi type="italic">line upon line,</hi> so loth we are to know the worst of ourselves. The sinners that are here to be exposed are <hi type="italic">two women,</hi> two kingdoms, sister-kingdoms, Israel and Judah, <hi type="italic">daughters of one mother,</hi> having been for a long time but <hi type="italic">one people.</hi> Solomon's kingdom was so large, so populous, that immediately after his death it divided into two. Observe, 1. Their character when they were one (<reference osisRef="Ezek.23.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">They committed whoredoms in Egypt,</hi> for there they were guilty of idolatry, as we read before, <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.8">ch. xx. 8</reference>. The representing of those sins which are most provoking to God and most ruining to a people by the sin of whoredom plainly intimates what an exceedingly sinful sin uncleanness is, how offensive, how destructive. Doubtless it is itself one of the worst of sins, for the worst of other sins are compared to it here and often elsewhere, which should increase our detestation and dread of all manner of <hi type="italic">fleshly lusts,</hi> all appearances of them and approaches to them, as <hi type="italic">warring against the soul,</hi> infatuating sinners, bewitching them, alienating their minds from God and all that is good, debauching conscience, rendering them odious in the eyes of the pure and holy God, and drowning them at last in destruction and perdition. 2. Their names when they became two, <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.4">v. 4</reference>. The kingdom of Israel is called the <hi type="italic">elder sister,</hi> because that first made the breach, and separated from the family both of kings and priests that God had appointed—the <hi type="italic">greater sister</hi> (so the word is), for ten tribes belonged to that kingdom and only two to the other. God says of them both, <hi type="italic">They were mine,</hi> for they were the seed of Abraham <hi type="italic">his friend</hi> and of Jacob <hi type="italic">his chosen;</hi> they were in covenant with God, and carried about with them the sign of <hi type="italic">their circumcision,</hi> the seal of the covenant. <hi type="italic">They were mine;</hi> and therefore their apostasy was the highest injustice. It was alienating God's property, it was the basest ingratitude to the best of benefactors, and a perfidious treacherous violation of the most sacred engagements. Note, Those who have been in profession the people of God, but have revolted from him, have a great deal to answer for more than those who never made any such profession. "<hi type="italic">They were mine;</hi> they were espoused to me, and to me <hi type="italic">they bore sons and daughters;</hi>" there were many among them that were devoted to God's honour, and employed in his service, and were the strength and beauty of these kingdoms, as children are of the families they are born in. In this parable Samaria and the kingdom of Israel shall bear the name of <hi type="italic">Aholah—her own tabernacle,</hi> because the places of worship which that kingdom had were of their own devising, their own choosing, and the worship itself was their own invention; God never owned it. <hi type="italic">Her tabernacle to herself</hi> (so some render it); "let her take it to herself, and make her best of it." Jerusalem and the kingdom of Judah bear the name of <hi type="italic">Aholibah—my tabernacle is in her,</hi> because <hi type="italic">their</hi> temple was the place which God himself had <hi type="italic">chosen</hi> to <hi type="italic">put his name there.</hi> He acknowledged it to be his, and honoured them with the tokens of his presence in it. Note, Of those that stand in relation to God, and make profession of his name, some have greater privileges and advantages than others; and, as those who have greater are thereby rendered the more inexcusable if they revolt from God, so those who have less will not thereby be rendered inexcusable. 3. The treacherous departure of the kingdom of Israel from God (<reference osisRef="Ezek.23.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">Aholah played the harlot when she was mine.</hi> Though the ten tribes had deserted the house of David, yet God owned them for <hi type="italic">his</hi> still; though Jeroboam, in setting up the golden calves, <hi type="italic">sinned, and made Israel to sin,</hi> yet, as long as they worshipped the God of Israel only, though by images, he did not quite cast them off. But the way of sin is down-hill. Aholah played the harlot, brought in the worship of Baal (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.16.31">1 Kings xvi. 31</reference>), set up that other god, that dunghill-god, in competition with Jehovah (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.21">1 Kings xviii. 21</reference>), as a vile adulteress <hi type="italic">dotes on her lovers,</hi> because they are well dressed and make a figure, because they are young and handsome (<reference osisRef="Ezek.23.6">v. 6</reference>), <hi type="italic">clothed with blue, captains and rulers, desirable young</hi> men, genteel, and that pass for men of honour, so she doted upon her neighbours, particularly the Assyrians, who had extended their conquests near them; she admired their idols and worshipped them, admired the pomp of their courts and their military strength and courted alliances with them upon any terms, as if her own God were not sufficient to be depended upon. We find one of the kings of Israel giving a <hi type="italic">thousand talents</hi> to the <hi type="italic">king of Assyria,</hi> to engage him in his interests, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.19">2 Kings xv. 19</reference>. She doted on the <hi type="italic">chosen men of Assyria,</hi> as worthy to be trusted and employed in the service of the state (<reference osisRef="Ezek.23.7">v. 7</reference>), and <hi type="italic">on all their idols with which she defiled herself.</hi> Note, Whatever creature we dote upon, pay homage to, and put a confidence in, we make an idol of that creature; and whatever we make an idol of we defile ourselves with. And now again the conviction looks back as far as the original of their nation: <hi type="italic">Neither left she her whoredoms which she brought from Egypt,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.8">v. 8</reference>. Their being idolaters in Egypt was a thing never to be forgotten—that they should be in love with Egypt's idols even when they were continually in fear of Egypt's tyrants and task-masters! But (as some have observed) therefore, at that time, when Satan boasted of his having <hi type="italic">walked through the earth</hi> as all his own, to disprove his pretensions God did not say, Hast thou considered <hi type="italic">my people Israel in Egypt?</hi> (for they had become idolaters, and were not to be boasted of), but, <hi type="italic">Hast thou considered my servant Job in the land of Uz?</hi> And this corrupt disposition in them, when they were first formed into a people, is an emblem of that original corruption which is born with us and is woven into our constitution, a strong bias towards the world and the flesh, like that in the Israelites towards idolatry; it was <hi type="italic">bred in the bone</hi> with them, and was charged upon them long after, that they <hi type="italic">left not their whoredoms brought from Egypt.</hi> It would never <hi type="italic">out of the flesh,</hi> though Egypt had been a house of bondage to them. Thus the corrupt affections and inclinations which we brought into the world with us we have not lost, nor got clear of, but still retain them, though the iniquity we were born in was the source of all the calamities which human life is liable to. 4. The destruction of the kingdom of Israel for their apostasy from God (<reference osisRef="Ezek.23.9-Ezek.23.10">v. 9, 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">I have delivered her into the hand of her lovers.</hi> God first justly gave her up to her lust (<hi type="italic">Ephraim is joined to idols, let him alone</hi>), and then gave her up <hi type="italic">to her lovers.</hi> The neighbouring nations, whose idolatries she had conformed to and whose friendship she had confided in, and in both had affronted God, are now made use of as the instruments of her destruction. The <hi type="italic">Assyrians, on whom she doted,</hi> soon spied out the <hi type="italic">nakedness of the land,</hi> discovered her blind side, on which to attack her, stripped her of all her ornaments and all her defences, and so <hi type="italic">uncovered</hi> her, and <hi type="italic">made her naked and bare,</hi> carried her <hi type="italic">sons and daughters</hi> into captivity, <hi type="italic">slew her with the sword,</hi> and quite destroyed that kingdom and put an end to it. We have the story at large <reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.6">2 Kings xvii. 6</reference>, &c., where the cause of the ruin of that once flourishing kingdom by the Assyrians is shown to be their forsaking the God of Israel, <hi type="italic">fearing other gods,</hi> and <hi type="italic">walking in the statutes of the heathen;</hi> it was for this that God was very <hi type="italic">angry with them and removed them out of his sight,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.18">v. 18</reference>. And that the Assyrians, whom they had been so fond of, should be employed in <hi type="italic">executing judgments</hi> upon them was very remarkable, and shows how God, in a way of righteous judgment, often makes that a scourge to sinners which they have inordinately set their hearts upon. The devil will for ever be a tormentor to those impenitent sinners who now hearken to him and comply with him as a tempter. Thus Samaria became <hi type="italic">famous among women,</hi> or <hi type="italic">infamous</hi> rather; she <hi type="italic">became a name</hi> (so the word is); not only she came to be the subject of discourse, and much talked of, as the desolations of cities and kingdoms fill the newspapers, but she was thus ruined for her idolatries <hi type="italic">in terrorem—for warning</hi> to all people to take heed of doing likewise; as the public execution of notorious malefactors makes them such <hi type="italic">a name,</hi> such an ill name, as may serve to frighten others from those wicked courses which have brought them to a miserable and shameful end. <reference osisRef="Deut.21.21">Deut. xxi. 21</reference>, <hi type="italic">All Israel shall hear and fear.</hi>
entries.74f22783849a2de3850561911547f174d71712d2: <div eID="gen18862" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Sins of Samaria and Jerusalem. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 591.)</title> <div sID="gen18863" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> And when her sister Aholibah saw <hi type="italic">this,</hi> she was more corrupt in her inordinate love than she, and in her whoredoms more than her sister in <hi type="italic">her</hi> whoredoms. <hi type="super">12</hi> She doted upon the Assyrians <hi type="italic">her</hi> neighbours, captains and rulers clothed most gorgeously, horsemen riding upon horses, all of them desirable young men. <hi type="super">13</hi> Then I saw that she was defiled, <hi type="italic">that</hi> they <hi type="italic">took</hi> both one way, <hi type="super">14</hi> And <hi type="italic">that</hi> she increased her whoredoms: for when she saw men portrayed upon the wall, the images of the Chaldeans portrayed with vermilion, <hi type="super">15</hi> Girded with girdles upon their loins, exceeding in dyed attire upon their heads, all of them princes to look to, after the manner of the Babylonians of Chaldea, the land of their nativity: <hi type="super">16</hi> And as soon as she saw them with her eyes, she doted upon them, and sent messengers unto them into Chaldea. <hi type="super">17</hi> And the Babylonians came to her into the bed of love, and they defiled her with their whoredom, and she was polluted with them, and her mind was alienated from them. <hi type="super">18</hi> So she discovered her whoredoms, and discovered her nakedness: then my mind was alienated from her, like as my mind was alienated from her sister. <hi type="super">19</hi> Yet she multiplied her whoredoms, in calling to remembrance the days of her youth, wherein she had played the harlot in the land of Egypt. <hi type="super">20</hi> For she doted upon their paramours, whose flesh <hi type="italic">is as</hi> the flesh of asses, and whose issue <hi type="italic">is like</hi> the issue of horses. <hi type="super">21</hi> Thus thou calledst to remembrance the lewdness of thy youth, in bruising thy teats by the Egyptians for the paps of thy youth. <div eID="gen18863" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18864" type="x-p"/> The prophet Hosea, in his time, observed that the two tribes retained their integrity, in a great measure, when the ten tribes had apostatized (<reference osisRef="Hos.11.12">Hos. xi. 12</reference>, <hi type="italic">Ephraim indeed compasses me about with lies, but Judah yet rules with God and is faithful with the saints;</hi> and this was justly expected from them: <reference osisRef="Hos.4.15">Hos. iv. 15</reference>, <hi type="italic">Though thou Israel play the harlot, yet let not Judah offend</hi>); but this lasted not long. By some unhappy matches made between the house of David and the house of Ahab the worship of Baal had been brought into the kingdom of Judah, but had been by the reforming kings worked out again; and at the time of the captivity of the ten tribes, which was in the reign of Hezekiah, things were in a good posture: but it lasted not long. In the reign of Manasseh, soon after the kingdom of Judah had seen the destruction of the kingdom of Israel, they became more corrupt than Israel had been in their inordinate love of idols, <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.11">v. 11</reference>. Instead of being made better by the warning which that destruction gave them, they were made worse by it, as if they were <hi type="italic">displeased because the Lord had made that breach upon Israel,</hi> and for that reason became disaffected to him and to his service. Instead of being made to stand in awe of him as a <hi type="italic">jealous God,</hi> they therefore grew strange to him, and liked those gods better that would admit of partners with them. Note, Those may justly expect God's judgments upon themselves who do not take warning by his judgments upon others, who see in others what is the end of sin and yet continue to make a light matter of it. But it is bad indeed with those who are made worse by that which should make them better, and have their lusts irritated and exasperated by that which was designed to suppress and subdue them. Jerusalem grew worse <hi type="italic">in her whoredoms</hi> than her sister Samaria had been <hi type="italic">in her whoredoms.</hi> This was observed before (<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.51">ch. xvi. 51</reference>), <hi type="italic">Neither has Samaria committed half of thy sins.</hi> <div eID="gen18864" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18865" type="x-p"/> I. Jerusalem, that had been a <hi type="italic">faithful city, became a harlot,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.1.21">Isa. i. 21</reference>. She also <hi type="italic">doted upon the Assyrians</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.23.12">v. 12</reference>), joined in league with them, joined in worship with them, grew to be in love with their <hi type="italic">captains and rulers,</hi> and cried them up as finer and more accomplished gentlemen than any that ever the land of Israel produced. "See how richly, how neatly, they are dressed, <hi type="italic">clothed most gorgeously;</hi> how well they sit a horse; they are <hi type="italic">horsemen riding on horses;</hi> how charmingly they look, <hi type="italic">all of them desirable young men.</hi>" And thus they grew to affect every thing that was foreign and to despise their own nation; and even the religion of it was mean and homely, and not to be compared with the curiosity and gaiety of the heathen temples. Thus she <hi type="italic">increased her whoredoms;</hi> she fell in love, fell in league, with the Chaldeans. Hezekiah himself was faulty this way when he was proud of the court which the king of Babylon made to him and complimented his ambassadors with the sight of all his treasures, <reference osisRef="Isa.39.2">Isa. xxxix. 2</reference>. And the humour increased (<reference osisRef="Ezek.23.14">v. 14</reference>); she doted upon the pictures of the Babylonian captains (<reference osisRef="Ezek.23.15-Ezek.23.16">v. 15, 16</reference>), joined in alliance with that kingdom, invited them to come and settle in Jerusalem, that they might refine the genius of the Jewish nation and make it more polite; nay, they sent for patterns of their images, altars, and temples, and made use of them in their worship. Thus was she <hi type="italic">polluted with her whoredoms</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.23.17">v. 17</reference>), and thereby she <hi type="italic">discovered her own whoredom</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.23.18">v. 18</reference>), her own strong inclination to idolatry. And when she had had enough of the Chaldeans, and grew tired of them and disposed to break her league with them, as Jehoiakim and Zedekiah did, <hi type="italic">her mind being alienated from them,</hi> she courted the <hi type="italic">Egyptians, doted upon their paramours</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.23.20">v. 20</reference>), would come into an alliance with them, and, to strengthen the alliance, would join with them in their idolatries and then depend upon them to be their protectors from all other nations; for so wise, so rich, so strong, was the Egyptian nation, and came to such perfection in idolatry, that there was no nation now which they could take such satisfaction in as in Egypt. Thus they <hi type="italic">called to remembrance the days of their youth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.23.19">v. 19</reference>), the <hi type="italic">lewdness of their youth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.21">v. 21</reference>. 1. They pleased themselves with the remembrance of it. When they began to set their affections upon Egypt, they encouraged themselves to put a confidence in that kingdom, because of the old acquaintance they had with it, as if they still retained the gust and relish of the <hi type="italic">leeks and onions</hi> they ate there, or rather of the idolatrous worship they learned there, and brought up with them thence. When they began an acquaintance with Egypt they remembered how merrily their fathers worshipped the golden calf, what music and dancing they had at that sport, which they learned in Egypt; and they hoped they should now have a fair pretence to come to that again. Thus <hi type="italic">she multiplied her whoredoms,</hi> repeated her former whoredoms, and encouraged herself to close with present temptations, by calling <hi type="italic">to remembrance the days of her youth.</hi> Note, Those who, instead of reflecting upon their former sins with sorrow and shame, reflect upon them with pleasure and pride, contract new guilt thereby, strengthen their own corruptions, and in effect bid defiance to repentance. This is returning <hi type="italic">with the dog to his vomit.</hi> 2. They called it <hi type="italic">God's remembrance,</hi> and provoked him to remember it against them. God had said indeed that he would reckon with them for <hi type="italic">the golden calf,</hi> that <hi type="italic">idol of Egypt</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.32.34">Exod. xxxii. 34</reference>); but such was his patience that he seemed to have forgotten it till they, by their league now with the Egyptians against the Chaldeans, did, as it were, put him in mind of it; and in the day <hi type="italic">when he visits he will now,</hi> as he has said, <hi type="italic">visit for that.</hi> It is very observable how this adulteress changes her lovers: she dotes first on the Assyrians; then she thought the Chaldeans finer and courted them; after a while her mind was alienated from them, and she thought the Egyptians more powerful (<reference osisRef="Ezek.23.20">v. 20</reference>) and she must contract an intimacy with them. This shows the folly, (1.) Of fleshly lusts; when they are indulged they grow humoursome and fickle, are soon surfeited but never satisfied; they must have variety, and what is loved one day is loathed the next. <hi type="italic">Unius adulterium matrimonium vocant—One adultery is called marriage,</hi> as Seneca observes. (2.) Of idolatry. Those who think one God too little will not think a hundred sufficient, but will still be for trying more, as finding all insufficient. (3.) Of seeking to creatures for help; we go from one to another, but are disappointed in them all, and can never rest till we have made the God of Israel our help. <div eID="gen18865" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18866" type="x-p"/> II. The faithful God justly gives a bill of divorce to this now faithless city, that has <hi type="italic">become a harlot.</hi> His jealousy soon discovered her lewdness (<reference osisRef="Ezek.23.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">I saw that she was defiled,</hi> that she was debauched, and saw which way her inclination was, that the <hi type="italic">two sisters both took one way,</hi> and that Jerusalem grew worse than Samaria. For, <hi type="italic">if we stretch out our hand to a strange god, will not God search this out?</hi> No doubt he will; and when he has found it can he be pleased with it? No (<reference osisRef="Ezek.23.18">v. 18</reference>): <hi type="italic">Then my mind was alienated from her, as it was from her sister.</hi> How could the pure and holy God any longer take delight in such a lewd generation? Note, Sin alienates God's mind from the sinner, and justly, for it is the alienation of the sinner's mind from God; but woe, and a thousand woes, to those from whom God's mind is alienated; for whom he turns from he will turn against.
entries.a730fe9a2ff9af92ca80b01292e25ee168da793e: <div eID="gen18866" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Punishment of Jerusalem. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 591.)</title> <div sID="gen18867" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">22</hi> Therefore, O Aholibah, thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ; Behold, I will raise up thy lovers against thee, from whom thy mind is alienated, and I will bring them against thee on every side; <hi type="super">23</hi> The Babylonians, and all the Chaldeans, Pekod, and Shoa, and Koa, <hi type="italic">and</hi> all the Assyrians with them: all of them desirable young men, captains and rulers, great lords and renowned, all of them riding upon horses. <hi type="super">24</hi> And they shall come against thee with chariots, waggons, and wheels, and with an assembly of people, <hi type="italic">which</hi> shall set against thee buckler and shield and helmet round about: and I will set judgment before them, and they shall judge thee according to their judgments. <hi type="super">25</hi> And I will set my jealousy against thee, and they shall deal furiously with thee: they shall take away thy nose and thine ears; and thy remnant shall fall by the sword: they shall take thy sons and thy daughters; and thy residue shall be devoured by the fire. <hi type="super">26</hi> They shall also strip thee out of thy clothes, and take away thy fair jewels. <hi type="super">27</hi> Thus will I make thy lewdness to cease from thee, and thy whoredom <hi type="italic">brought</hi> from the land of Egypt: so that thou shalt not lift up thine eyes unto them, nor remember Egypt any more. <hi type="super">28</hi> For thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ; Behold, I will deliver thee into the hand <hi type="italic">of them</hi> whom thou hatest, into the hand <hi type="italic">of them</hi> from whom thy mind is alienated: <hi type="super">29</hi> And they shall deal with thee hatefully, and shall take away all thy labour, and shall leave thee naked and bare: and the nakedness of thy whoredoms shall be discovered, both thy lewdness and thy whoredoms. <hi type="super">30</hi> I will do these <hi type="italic">things</hi> unto thee, because thou hast gone a whoring after the heathen, <hi type="italic">and</hi> because thou art polluted with their idols. <hi type="super">31</hi> Thou hast walked in the way of thy sister; therefore will I give her cup into thine hand. <hi type="super">32</hi> Thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ; Thou shalt drink of thy sister's cup deep and large: thou shalt be laughed to scorn and had in derision; it containeth much. <hi type="super">33</hi> Thou shalt be filled with drunkenness and sorrow, with the cup of astonishment and desolation, with the cup of thy sister Samaria. <hi type="super">34</hi> Thou shalt even drink it and suck <hi type="italic">it</hi> out, and thou shalt break the sherds thereof, and pluck off thine own breasts: for I have spoken <hi type="italic">it,</hi> saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> . <hi type="super">35</hi> Therefore thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ; Because thou hast forgotten me, and cast me behind thy back, therefore bear thou also thy lewdness and thy whoredoms. <div eID="gen18867" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18868" type="x-p"/> Jerusalem stands indicted by the name of <hi type="italic">Aholibah,</hi> for that she, as a false traitor to her sovereign Lord the God of heaven, not having his fear before her eyes, but moved by the instigation of the devil, had revolted from her allegiance to him, had compassed and imagined to shake off his government, had kept up a correspondence had joined in confederacy with his enemies, and the pretenders to a deity, in contempt of his crown and dignity. To this indictment she has pleaded, Not guilty: <hi type="italic">I am not polluted; I have not gone after Baalim.</hi> But it is found against her by the notorious evidence of the fact, and she stands convicted of it, nor has any thing material to offer why judgment should not be given and execution awarded according to law. In these verses, therefore, we have the sentence. <div eID="gen18868" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18869" type="x-p"/> I. Her old confederates must be her executioners; and those whom she had courted to be her leaders in sin are now to be employed as instruments of her punishment (<reference osisRef="Ezek.23.22">v. 22</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I will raise up thy lovers against thee,</hi> the Chaldeans, whom formerly thou didst so much admire and covet an acquaintance with, but from whom thy mind is since alienated and with whom thou hast perfidiously broken covenant." They are called <hi type="italic">thy lovers</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.23.22">v. 22</reference>) and yet (<reference osisRef="Ezek.23.28">v. 28</reference>) <hi type="italic">those whom thou hatest.</hi> Note, It is common for sinful love soon to turn into hatred; as Amnon's to Tamar. Those of headstrong and unreasonable passions are often very hot against those persons and things that a little before they were as hot for. Fools run into extremes; nay, and wise men may see cause to change their sentiments. And therefore, as we should rejoice and weep as if we rejoiced not and wept not, so we should love and hate as if we loved not and hated not. <hi type="italic">Ita ama tanquam osurus—Love as one who may have cause to feel aversion.</hi> <div eID="gen18869" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18870" type="x-p"/> II. The execution to be done upon her is very terrible. <div eID="gen18870" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18871" type="x-p"/> 1. Her enemies shall come against her <hi type="italic">on every side</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.23.22">v. 22</reference>), those of the several nations that constituted the Chaldean army (<reference osisRef="Ezek.23.23">v. 23</reference>), all of them <hi type="italic">great lords and renowned,</hi> whose pomp, and grandeur, and splendid appearance made them look the more amiable when they came as friends to protect and patronise Jerusalem, but the more formidable when they came to chastise its treachery and aimed at no less than its ruin. (1.) They shall come with a great deal of military force (<reference osisRef="Ezek.23.24">v. 24</reference>), with <hi type="italic">chariots and wagons</hi> furnished with all necessary provisions for a camp, with arms and ammunition, bag and baggage, with a vast army, and well armed. (2.) They shall have justice on their side: "<hi type="italic">I will set judgment before them</hi>" (they shall have right with them as well as might; for the king of Babylon had just cause to make war upon the king of Judah, because he had broken his league with him), "and therefore they <hi type="italic">shall judge thee,</hi> not only according to God's judgments, as the instruments of his justice, to punish thee for the indignities done to him, but <hi type="italic">according to their judgments,</hi> according to the law of nations, to punish thee for thy perfidious dealings with them." (3.) They shall prosecute the war with a great deal of fury and resentment. It being a war of revenge, <hi type="italic">they shall deal with thee hatefully,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.29">v. 29</reference>. This will make the execution the more severe that their swords will be dipped in poison. Thou hatest them, and they shall deal hatefully with thee; those that hate will be hated and will be hatefully dealt with. (4.) God himself will lead them on, and his anger shall be mingled with theirs (<reference osisRef="Ezek.23.25">v. 25</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will set my jealousy against thee;</hi> that shall kindle this fire, and then <hi type="italic">they shall deal furiously with thee.</hi> If men deal ever so hatefully, ever so furiously, with us, yet, if we have God on our side, we need not fear them; they can do us no real hurt. But if men deal furiously with us, and God set his jealousy against us too, what will become of us? <div eID="gen18871" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18872" type="x-p"/> 2. The particulars of the sentence here passed upon this notorious adulteress are, (1.) That all she has shall be seized on. The <hi type="italic">clothes</hi> and the <hi type="italic">fair jewels,</hi> with which she had endeavoured to recommend herself to her lovers, these she shall be stripped of, <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.26">v. 26</reference>. All those things that were the ornaments of their state shall be taken away: "<hi type="italic">They shall take away all thy labour,</hi> all that thou hast gotten by thy labour, and shall <hi type="italic">leave thee naked and bare,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.29">v. 29</reference>. Both city and country shall be impoverished and all the wealth of both swept away. (2.) That her children shall go into captivity. "They shall <hi type="italic">take thy sons and thy daughters,</hi> and make slaves of them (<reference osisRef="Ezek.23.25">v. 25</reference>); for they are <hi type="italic">children of whoredoms,</hi> unworthy the dignities and privileges of Israelites," <reference osisRef="Hos.2.4">Hos. ii. 4</reference>. (3.) That she shall be stigmatized and deformed: "They shall <hi type="italic">take away thy nose and thy ears,</hi> shall mark thee for a harlot, and render thee for ever odious," <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.25">v. 25</reference>. This intimates the many cruelties of the Chaldean soldiers towards the Jews that fell into their hands, whom, it is probable, they used barbarously. Some will have this to be understood figuratively; and by the nose they think is meant the kingly dignity, and by the ears that of the priesthood. (4.) That she shall be exposed to shame: <hi type="italic">Thy lewdness and thy whoredoms shall be discovered</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.23.29">v. 29</reference>), as, when a malefactor is punished, all his crimes are ripped up, and repeated to his disgrace; what was secret then comes to light, and what was done long since is then called to mind. (5.) That she shall be quite cut off and ruined: "The <hi type="italic">remnant</hi> of thy people that have escaped the famine and pestilence shall fall <hi type="italic">by the sword;</hi> and the residue of thy houses that have not been battered down about thy ears shall be <hi type="italic">devoured by the fire,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.25">v. 25</reference>. And this shall be the end of Jerusalem. <div eID="gen18872" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18873" type="x-p"/> III. Because she has trod in the steps of Samaria's sins, she must expect no other than Samaria's fate. It is common, in giving judgment, to have an eye to precedents; so has God in passing this sentence on Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Ezek.23.31">v. 31</reference>, &c.): "<hi type="italic">Thou hast walked in the way of thy sister,</hi> notwithstanding the warning thou hast had given thee, by the fatal consequences of her wickedness; and therefore I <hi type="italic">will give her cup,</hi> her portion of miseries, <hi type="italic">into thy hand,</hi> the cup of the Lord's fury, which will be to thee a <hi type="italic">cup of trembling.</hi>" Now, 1. This cup is said to be <hi type="italic">deep and large,</hi> and to <hi type="italic">contain much</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.23.32">v. 32</reference>), abundance of God's wrath and abundance of miseries, the fruits of that wrath. It is such a cup as that which we read of, <reference osisRef="Jer.25.15-Jer.25.16">Jer. xxv. 15, 16</reference>. The cup of divine vengeance holds a great deal, and so those will find into whose hand it shall be put. 2. They shall be made to drink the very dregs of this cup, as the <hi type="italic">wicked</hi> are said to do (<reference osisRef="Ps.75.8">Ps. lxxv. 8</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Thou shalt drink it and suck it out,</hi> not because it is pleasant, but because it is forced upon thee (<reference osisRef="Ezek.23.34">v. 34</reference>); <hi type="italic">thou shalt break the shreds thereof,</hi> and <hi type="italic">pluck off thy own breasts,</hi> for indignation at the extreme bitterness of this cup, being <hi type="italic">full of the fury of the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.51.20">Isa. li. 20</reference>), as men in great anguish tear their hair, and throw every thing from them. Finding there is no remedy, but it must be drank (for <hi type="italic">I have spoken it, saith the Lord God</hi>), thou shalt have no manner of patience in the drinking of it." 3. They shall be intoxicated by it, made sick, and be at their wits' end, as men in drink are, staggering, and stumbling, and ready to fall (<reference osisRef="Ezek.23.33">v. 33</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou shalt be filled with drunkenness and sorrow.</hi> Note, Drunkenness has sorrow attending it, to such a degree that the utmost confusion and astonishment are here represented by it. Who would think that that which is such a force upon nature, such a scandal to it, which deprives men of their reason, disorders them to the last degree, and is therefore expressive of the greatest misery, should yet be with many a beloved sin, that they should damn their own souls to distemper their own bodies? <hi type="italic">Who has woe</hi> and <hi type="italic">sorrow</hi> like them? <reference osisRef="Prov.23.29">Prov. xxiii. 29</reference>. 4. Being so intoxicated, they shall become, as drunkards deserve to be, a laughing-stock to all about them (<reference osisRef="Ezek.23.32">v. 32</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou shalt be laughed to scorn and had in derision,</hi> as acting ridiculously in every thing thou goest about. When God is about to ruin a people he <hi type="italic">makes their judges fools</hi> and <hi type="italic">pours contempt on their princes,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.12.17">Job xii. 17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.12.21">21</reference>. <div eID="gen18873" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18874" type="x-p"/> IV. In all this God will be justified, and by all this they will be reformed; and so the issue even of this will be God's glory and their good. 1. They have been bad, very bad, and that justifies God in all that is brought upon them (<reference osisRef="Ezek.23.30">v. 30</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will do these things unto thee because thou hast gone a whoring after the heathen,</hi> and (<reference osisRef="Ezek.23.35">v. 35</reference>) <hi type="italic">because thou hast forgotten me and cast me behind thy back.</hi> Note, Forgetfulness of God, and a contempt of him, of his eye upon us and authority over us, are at the bottom of all our treacherous adulterous departures from him. <hi type="italic">Therefore</hi> men wander after idols, because they forget <hi type="italic">God,</hi> and their obligations to him; nor could they look with so much desire and delight upon the baits of sin if they did not first cast God <hi type="italic">behind their back,</hi> as not worthy to be regarded. And those who put such an affront upon God, how can they think but that it should turn upon themselves at last? <hi type="italic">Therefore bear thou also thy lewdness and thy whoredoms;</hi> that is, thou shalt <hi type="italic">suffer the punishment</hi> of them, and thou alone must <hi type="italic">bear the blame.</hi> Men need no more to sink them than the weight of their own sins; and those who will not part with their lewdness and their whoredoms must bear them. 2. They shall be better, much better, and this fire, though consuming to many, shall be refining to a remnant (<reference osisRef="Ezek.23.27">v. 27</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thus will I make thy lewdness to cease from thee.</hi> The judgments which were brought upon them by their sins parted between them and their sins, and taught them at length to say, <hi type="italic">What have we to do any more with idols?</hi> Observe, (1.) How inveterate the disease was: <hi type="italic">Thy whoredoms were brought from the land of Egypt.</hi> Their disposition to idolatry was early and innate, their practice of it was ancient, and had gained a sort of prescription by long usage. (2.) How complete the cure was notwithstanding: "Though it has taken root, yet it shall be made to cease, so that thou shalt not so much as <hi type="italic">lift up thy eyes</hi> to the idols again, nor <hi type="italic">remember Egypt</hi> with pleasure <hi type="italic">any more.</hi>" They shall avoid the occasions of this sin, for they shall not so much as look upon an idol, lest their hearts should unawares <hi type="italic">walk after their eyes.</hi> And they shall abandon all inclinations to it: "They shall <hi type="italic">not remember Egypt;</hi> they shall not retain any of that affection for idols which they had from the very infancy of their nation." They got it, through the corruption of nature, in their bondage in Egypt, and lost it, through the grace of God, in their captivity in Babylon, which this was the blessed fruit of, even <hi type="italic">the taking away of sin,</hi> of <hi type="italic">that</hi> sin; so that whereas, before the captivity, no nation (all things considered) was more impetuously bent upon idols and idolatry than they were, after that captivity no nation was more vehemently set against idols and idolatry than they were, insomuch that at this day the image-worship which is practised in the church of Rome confirms the Jews as much as any thing in their prejudices against the Christian religion.
entries.81b3d86d129a619f285025ffabcac86826f6eff4: <div eID="gen18874" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Israel and Judah Accused; Judgments Predicted. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 591.)</title> <div sID="gen18875" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">36</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said moreover unto me; Son of man, wilt thou judge Aholah and Aholibah? yea, declare unto them their abominations; <hi type="super">37</hi> That they have committed adultery, and blood <hi type="italic">is</hi> in their hands, and with their idols have they committed adultery, and have also caused their sons, whom they bare unto me, to pass for them through <hi type="italic">the fire,</hi> to devour <hi type="italic">them.</hi> <hi type="super">38</hi> Moreover this they have done unto me: they have defiled my sanctuary in the same day, and have profaned my sabbaths. <hi type="super">39</hi> For when they had slain their children to their idols, then they came the same day into my sanctuary to profane it; and, lo, thus have they done in the midst of mine house. <hi type="super">40</hi> And furthermore, that ye have sent for men to come from far, unto whom a messenger <hi type="italic">was</hi> sent; and, lo, they came: for whom thou didst wash thyself, paintedst thy eyes, and deckedst thyself with ornaments, <hi type="super">41</hi> And satest upon a stately bed, and a table prepared before it, whereupon thou hast set mine incense and mine oil. <hi type="super">42</hi> And a voice of a multitude being at ease <hi type="italic">was</hi> with her: and with the men of the common sort <hi type="italic">were</hi> brought Sabeans from the wilderness, which put bracelets upon their hands, and beautiful crowns upon their heads. <hi type="super">43</hi> Then said I unto <hi type="italic">her that was</hi> old in adulteries, Will they now commit whoredoms with her, and she <hi type="italic">with them?</hi> <hi type="super">44</hi> Yet they went in unto her, as they go in unto a woman that playeth the harlot: so went they in unto Aholah and unto Aholibah, the lewd women. <hi type="super">45</hi> And the righteous men, they shall judge them after the manner of adulteresses, and after the manner of women that shed blood; because they <hi type="italic">are</hi> adulteresses, and blood <hi type="italic">is</hi> in their hands. <hi type="super">46</hi> For thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ; I will bring up a company upon them, and will give them to be removed and spoiled. <hi type="super">47</hi> And the company shall stone them with stones, and dispatch them with their swords; they shall slay their sons and their daughters, and burn up their houses with fire. <hi type="super">48</hi> Thus will I cause lewdness to cease out of the land, that all women may be taught not to do after your lewdness. <hi type="super">49</hi> And they shall recompense your lewdness upon you, and ye shall bear the sins of your idols: and ye shall know that I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> . <div eID="gen18875" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18876" type="x-p"/> After the ten tribes were carried into captivity, and that kingdom was made quite desolate, the remains of it by degrees incorporated with the kingdom of Judah, and gained a settlement (many of them) in Jerusalem; so that the <hi type="italic">two sisters</hi> had in effect become <hi type="italic">one</hi> again; and therefore, in these verses, the prophet takes those to task jointly who were thus conjoined: "<hi type="italic">Wilt thou judge Aholah and Aholibah</hi> together? <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.36">v. 36</reference>. Wilt thou go about to frame an excuse for them? Thou seest the matter is so bad as not to bear an excuse." Or, rather, "Thou shalt now be employed, in God's name, to <hi type="italic">judge them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.4">ch. xx. 4</reference>. The matter is rather worse than better since the union." <div eID="gen18876" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18877" type="x-p"/> I. Let them be made to see the sins they are guilty of: <hi type="italic">Declare unto them</hi> openly and boldly <hi type="italic">their abominations.</hi> 1. They have been guilty of gross idolatry, here called <hi type="italic">adultery. With their idols they have committed adultery</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.23.37">v. 37</reference>), have broken their marriage-covenant with God, have lusted after the gratifications of a carnal sensual mind in the worship of God. This is the first and worst of the abominations he is to charge them with. 2. They have committed the most barbarous murders, in sacrificing their children to Moloch, a sin so unnatural that they deserve to hear of it upon all occasions: <hi type="italic">Blood is in their hands,</hi> innocent blood, the blood of their own children, which they have <hi type="italic">caused to pass through the fire</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.23.37">v. 37</reference>), not that they might be dedicated to the idols, but that they might be devoured, a sign that they loved their idols better than that which was dearest to them in the world. 3. They have profaned the sacred things with which God had dignified and distinguished them: This <hi type="italic">they have done unto me,</hi> this indignity, this injury, <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.38">v. 38</reference>. Every contempt put upon that which is holy reflects upon him who is the fountain of holiness, and from a relation to whom whatever is called holy has its denomination. God had set up his sanctuary among them, but they defiled it, by making it a house of merchandise, a den of thieves; nay, and much worse; there they set up their idols and worshipped them, and there they shed the blood of God's prophets. God had revealed to them his holy sabbaths, but they profaned them, by doing all manner of servile work therein, or perhaps by sports and recreations on that day, not only practised, but allowed and encouraged by authority. They <hi type="italic">defiled the sanctuary</hi> on <hi type="italic">the same day</hi> that they <hi type="italic">profaned the sabbath.</hi> To defile the sanctuary was bad enough on any day, but to do it on the sabbath day was an aggravation. We commonly say, <hi type="italic">The better day the better deed;</hi> but here, the better day the worse deed. God takes notice of the circumstances of sin which add to the guilt. He shows (<reference osisRef="Ezek.23.39">v. 39</reference>) what was their profanation both of the sanctuary and of the sabbath. <hi type="italic">They slew their children,</hi> and sacrificed them <hi type="italic">to their idols,</hi> to the great dishonour both of God and of human nature; and then came, on <hi type="italic">the same day,</hi> their hands imbrued with the blood of their children and their clothes stained with it, to attend in <hi type="italic">God's sanctuary,</hi> not to ask pardon for what they had done, but to present themselves before him, as other Israelites did, expecting acceptance with him, notwithstanding these villanies which they were guilty of; as if God either did not know their wickedness or did not hate it. Thus they <hi type="italic">profaned the sanctuary,</hi> as if that were a protection to the worst of malefactors; for thus they did <hi type="italic">in the midst of his house.</hi> Note, It is a profanation of God's solemn ordinances when those that are grossly and openly profane and vicious impudently and impenitently so intrude upon the services and privileges of them. <hi type="italic">Give not that which is holy unto dogs. Friend, how camest thou in hither?</hi> 4. They have courted foreign alliances, been proud of them, and reposed a confidence in them. This also is represented by the sin of adultery, for it was a departure from God, not only <hi type="italic">to whom</hi> alone they ought to pay their homage and not to idols, but <hi type="italic">in</hi> whom alone they ought to put their trust, and not in creatures. Israel was a peculiar people, must <hi type="italic">dwell alone</hi> and not be <hi type="italic">reckoned among the nations;</hi> and they profane their crown, and lay their honour in the dust, when they covet to be like them or in <hi type="italic">league</hi> with them. But this they have now done; they have entered into strict alliances with the Assyrians, Chaldeans, and Egyptians, the most renowned and potent kingdoms at that time; but they scorned alliances with the petty kingdoms and states that lay near them, which yet might have been of more real service to them. Note, Affecting an acquaintance and correspondence with great people has often been a snare to good people. Let us see how Jerusalem courts her high allies, thinking thereby to make herself considerable. (1.) She privately requested that a public embassy might be sent to her (<reference osisRef="Ezek.23.40">v. 40</reference>): You <hi type="italic">sent a messenger for men to come from far.</hi> It seems, then, that the neighbours had no desire to come into a confederacy with Jerusalem, but she thrust herself upon them, and sent under-hand to desire them to court her: and, <hi type="italic">lo, they came.</hi> The wisest and best may be drawn unavoidably into company and conversation with profane and wicked people: but it is no sign either of wisdom or goodness to covet an intimacy with such and to court it. (2.) Great preparation was made for the reception of these foreign ministers, for their public entry and public audience, which is compared to the pains that an adulteress takes to make herself look handsome. Jezebel-like, thou <hi type="italic">paintedst thy face</hi> and <hi type="italic">deckedst thyself with ornaments,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.40">v. 40</reference>. The king and princes made themselves new clothes, fitted up the rooms of state, beautified the furniture, and made it look fresh. Thou <hi type="italic">sattest upon a stately bed</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.23.41">v. 41</reference>), a stately throne; <hi type="italic">a table was prepared, whereon thou has set my oil and my incense.</hi> This was either, [1.] A feast for the ambassadors, a noble treat, agreeable to the other preparations. There was incense to perfume the room and oil to anoint their heads. Or, [2.] An altar already furnished for the ambassadors' use in the worship of their idols, to let them know that the Israelites were not so strait-laced but that they could allow foreigners the free exercise of their religion among them, and furnish them with chapels, yea, and complimented them so far as to join with them in their devotions; though the law of their God was against it, yet they could easily dispense with themselves to oblige a friend. The oil and incense God calls <hi type="italic">his,</hi> not only because they were the gift of his providence, but because they should have been offered at his altar, which was an aggravation of their sin in serving idols and idolaters with them. See <reference osisRef="Hos.2.8">Hos. ii. 8</reference>. (3.) There was great joy at their coming, as if it were such a blessing as never happened to Jerusalem before (<reference osisRef="Ezek.23.42">v. 42</reference>): <hi type="italic">A voice of a multitude being at ease was with her.</hi> The people were very easy, for they thought themselves very safe and happy now that they had such powerful allies; and therefore attended the ambassadors with loud huzzas and acclamations of joy. A great confluence of people there was to the court upon this occasion. The <hi type="italic">men of the common sort</hi> were there to grace the solemnity, and to increase the crowd; and <hi type="italic">with them were brought Sabeans from the wilderness.</hi> The margin reads it <hi type="italic">drunkards from the wilderness,</hi> that would drink healths to the prosperity of this grand alliance, and force them upon others, and be most noisy in shouting upon this occasion. Whoever they were, in honour of the ambassadors they put <hi type="italic">bracelets upon their hands and beautiful crowns upon their heads,</hi> which made the cavalcade appear very splendid. (4.) God by his prophets warned them against making these dangerous leagues with foreigners (<reference osisRef="Ezek.23.43">v. 43</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Then said I unto her that was old in adulteries,</hi> that from the first was fond of leagues with the heathen, of matching with their families (<reference osisRef="Judg.3.6">Judg. iii. 6</reference>), and afterwards of making alliances with their kingdoms, and, though often disappointed therein, would never be dissuaded from it (this was the adultery she was old in), I said, <hi type="italic">Will they now commit whoredoms with her and she with them?</hi> Surely experience and observation will by this time have convinced both them and her that an alliance between the nation of the Jews and a heathen nation can never be for the advantage of either." They are <hi type="italic">iron and clay,</hi> that will not mix, nor will God bless such an alliance, or smile upon it. But, it seems, her being old in these adulteries, instead of weaning her from them, as one would expect, does but make her the more impudent and insatiable in them; for, though she was thus admonished of the folly of it, <hi type="italic">yet they went in unto her,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.44">v. 44</reference>. A bargain was soon clapped up, and a league made, first with this, and then with the other, foreign state. Samaria did so, Jerusalem did so, like lewd women. They could not rest satisfied in the embraces of God's laws and care, and the assurances of protection he gave them; they could not think his covenant with them security enough. But they must by treaties and leagues, politic ones (they thought) and well-concerted, throw themselves into the arms of foreign princes, and put their interests under their protection. Note, Those hearts go a whoring from God that take a complacency in the pomp of the world and put a confidence in its wealth, and in an <hi type="italic">arm of flesh,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.17.5">Jer. xvii. 5</reference>. <div eID="gen18877" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18878" type="x-p"/> II. Let them be made to foresee the judgments that are coming upon them for these sins (<reference osisRef="Ezek.23.45">v. 45</reference>): <hi type="italic">The righteous men, they shall judge them.</hi> Some make the instruments of their destruction to be the righteous men that shall judge them. The Assyrians that destroyed Samaria, the Chaldeans that destroyed Jerusalem, those were comparatively righteous, had a sense of justice between man and man and justly resented the treachery of the Jewish nation; however, they executed God's judgments, which, we are sure, are all righteous. Others understand it of the prophets, whose office it was, in God's name, to judge them and pass sentence upon them. Or we may take it as an appeal to all righteous men, to all that have a sense of equity; they shall all judge concerning these cities, and agree in their verdict, that forasmuch as they have been notoriously guilty of adultery and murder, and the guilt is national, therefore they ought to suffer the pains and penalties which by law are inflicted upon women in their personal capacity that shed blood and are adulteresses. Righteous men will say, "Why should bloody filthy cities escape any better than bloody filthy persons? <hi type="italic">Judge, I pray thee,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Isa.5.3">Isa. v. 3</reference>. This judgment being given by the righteous men, the righteous God will award execution. See here, 1. What the execution will be, <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.46-Ezek.23.47">v. 46, 47</reference>. The same as before, <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.23">v. 23</reference>, &c. God will <hi type="italic">bring a company</hi> of enemies <hi type="italic">upon them,</hi> who shall be made to serve his holy purposes even when they are serving their own sinful appetites and passions. These enemies shall easily prevail, for God will <hi type="italic">give them</hi> into their hands <hi type="italic">to be removed and spoiled;</hi> this company shall <hi type="italic">stone them with stones</hi> as malefactors, shall <hi type="italic">single them out</hi> and <hi type="italic">dispatch them with their swords;</hi> and, as was sometimes done in severe executions (witness that of Achan), they shall <hi type="italic">slay their children and burn their houses.</hi> 2. What will be the effects of it. (1.) Thus they shall suffer for their sins: Their <hi type="italic">lewdness shall be recompensed upon them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.23.49">v. 49</reference>); and they shall <hi type="italic">bear the sins of their idols,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.35">v. 35</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.39">49</reference>. Thus God will assert the honour of his broken law and injured government, and let the world know what a just and jealous God he is. (2.) Thus they shall be broken off from their sins: <hi type="italic">I will cause lewdness to cease out of the land,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.27">v. 27</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.48">48</reference>. The destruction of God's city, like the death of God's saints, shall do that for them which ordinances and providences before could not do; it shall quite take away their sin, so that Jerusalem shall rise out of its ashes a new lump, as gold comes out of the furnace purified from its dross. (3.) Thus other cities and nations will have fair warning given them to keep themselves from idols. That <hi type="italic">all women may be taught not to do after your lewdness.</hi> This is the end of the punishment of malefactors, that they may be made examples to others, who will <hi type="italic">see and fear. Smite the scorner and the simple will beware.</hi> The judgments of God upon some are designed to teach others, and happy are those who receive instruction from them not to tread in the steps of sinners, lest they be taken in their snares; those who would be taught this must <hi type="italic">know God is the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.23.49">v. 49</reference>), that he is the governor of the world, a God that judges in the earth, and with whom there is <hi type="italic">no respect of persons.</hi>  <chapter eID="Ezek.23"/> <div eID="gen18878" type="x-p"/>

entries.e9bed3ac9b79e9619dd82291fe63c0531c84eb3e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11420"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 23</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ezek.23.1-Ezek.23.49">Eze 23:1-49</reference>. Israel's and Judah's Sin and Punishment Are Parabolically Portrayed under the Names Aholah and Aholibah.</title> <div sID="gen20670" type="x-p"/> The imagery is similar to that in the sixteenth chapter; but here the reference is not as there so much to the breach of the spiritual marriage covenant with God by the people's idolatries, as by their worldly spirit, and their trusting to alliances with the heathen for safety, rather than to God.<div eID="gen20670" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20671" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11420"/><hi type="bold">2. two ... of one mother--</hi>Israel and Judah, one nation by birth from the same ancestress, Sarah. <div eID="gen20671" type="x-p"/>
entries.8332149a9ff9ade495648adacffff6ed2abba9fa: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11421"/><div sID="gen20672" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11421"/>3. Even so early in their history as their Egyptian sojourn, they committed idolatries (see on <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.6-Ezek.20.8">Eze 20:6-8</reference>; Joshua 24. 14).<div eID="gen20672" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20673" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in their youth--</hi>an aggravation of their sin. It was at the very time of their receiving extraordinary favors from God (<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.6">Eze 16:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.22">22</reference>).<div eID="gen20673" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20674" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they bruised--</hi>namely, the Egyptians. <div eID="gen20674" type="x-p"/>
entries.63054d3efbc298cfb22efe19f162f3558f3853f4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11422"/><div sID="gen20675" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11422"/><hi type="bold">4. Aholah--</hi>that is, "Her tent" (put for worship, as the first worship of God in Israel was in a tent or tabernacle), as contrasted with Aholibah, that is, "My tent in her." The Beth-el worship of Samaria was of her own devising, not of God's appointment; the temple-worship of Jerusalem was expressly appointed by Jehovah, who "dwelt" there, "setting up His tabernacle among the people as His" (<reference osisRef="Exod.25.8">Ex 25:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.26.11">Le 26:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.12">12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.22.19">Jos 22:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.76.2">Psa 76:2</reference>).<div eID="gen20675" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20676" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the elder--</hi>Samaria is called "the elder" because she preceded Judah in her apostasy and its punishment.<div eID="gen20676" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20677" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they were mine--</hi>Previous to apostasy under Jeroboam, Samaria (Israel, or the ten tribes), equally with Judah, worshipped the true God. God therefore never renounced the right over Israel, but sent prophets, as Elijah and Elisha, to declare His will to them. <div eID="gen20677" type="x-p"/>
entries.8157d22e8dbc8a644b354dd8fb88ea82eecb7bd2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11423"/><div sID="gen20678" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11423"/><hi type="bold">5. when ... mine--</hi>literally, "under Me," that is, subject to Me as her lawful husband.<div eID="gen20678" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20679" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">neighbours--</hi>On the northeast the kingdom of Israel bordered on that of Assyria; for the latter had occupied much of Syria. Their neighborhood in locality was emblematical of their being near in corruption of morals and worship. The alliances of Israel with Assyria, which are the chief subject of reprobation here, tended to this (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.19">2Ki 15:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.16.7">16:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.16.9">9</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.3">17:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.8.9">Ho 8:9</reference>). <div eID="gen20679" type="x-p"/>
entries.04921504917f2d5f963fc683c322714ef93222f1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11424"/><div sID="gen20680" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11424"/><hi type="bold">6. blue--</hi>rather, "purple" [Fairbairn]. As a lustful woman's passions are fired by showy dress and youthful appearance in men, so Israel was seduced by the pomp and power of Assyria (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.10.8">Is 10:8</reference>).<div eID="gen20680" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20681" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">horsemen--</hi>cavaliers. <div eID="gen20681" type="x-p"/>
entries.4c1e071c8845aa52f281438847bcc1029daaa84e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11425"/><div sID="gen20682" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11425"/><hi type="bold">7. all their idols--</hi>There was nothing that she refused to her lovers. <div eID="gen20682" type="x-p"/>
entries.c622bbd9f22377dfa061e8b0b4441d07ded06810: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11426"/><div sID="gen20683" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11426"/><hi type="bold">8. whoredoms brought from Egypt--</hi>the calves set up in Dan and Beth-el by Jeroboam, answering to the Egyptian bull-formed idol Apis. Her alliances with Egypt politically are also meant (<reference osisRef="Isa.30.2">Is 30:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.30.3">3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.31.1">31:1</reference>). The ten tribes probably resumed the Egyptian rites, in order to enlist the Egyptians against Judah (<reference osisRef="2Chr.12.2-2Chr.12.4">2Ch 12:2-4</reference>). <div eID="gen20683" type="x-p"/>
entries.3536adee2b1b438a344870fc502e92d27184e171: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11427"/><div sID="gen20684" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11427"/>9. God, in righteous retribution, turned their objects of trust into the instruments of their punishment: Pul, Tiglath-pileser, Esar-haddon, and Shalmaneser (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.19">2Ki 15:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.29">29</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.3">17:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.6.24">6, 24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezra.4.2">Ezr 4:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezra.4.10">10</reference>). "It was their sin to have sought after such lovers, and it was to be their punishment that these lovers should become their destroyers" [Fairbairn]. <div eID="gen20684" type="x-p"/>
entries.01d4d57f222ee3603c64f085da4767499ef7b95b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11428"/><div sID="gen20685" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11428"/><hi type="bold">10. became famous--</hi>literally, "she became a name," that is, as notorious by her punishment as she had been by her sins, so as to be quoted as a warning to others.<div eID="gen20685" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20686" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">women--</hi>that is, neighboring peoples. <div eID="gen20686" type="x-p"/>
entries.1ddf86a249aada8d6ccf935795dc235509b35f58: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11429"/><div sID="gen20687" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11429"/>11. Judah, the southern kingdom, though having the "warning" (see on <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.10">Eze 23:10</reference>) of the northern kingdom before her eyes, instead of profiting by it, went to even greater lengths in corruption than Israel. Her greater spiritual privileges made her guilt the greater (<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.47">Eze 16:47</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.51">51</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.3.11">Jr 3:11</reference>). <div eID="gen20687" type="x-p"/>
entries.f2a25166e8f267bc3c51a9b37b4f3b81ec361f0a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11430"/><div sID="gen20688" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11430"/>12. (<reference osisRef="Ezek.23.6">Eze 23:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.23">23</reference>).<div eID="gen20688" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20689" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">most gorgeously--</hi>literally, "to perfection." Grotius translates, "wearing a crown," or "chaplet," such as lovers wore in visiting their mistresses. <div eID="gen20689" type="x-p"/>
entries.9c1028b7b19cb9d5847f9eaf030f48c2867a6a4b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11431"/><div sID="gen20690" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11431"/><hi type="bold">13. one way--</hi>both alike forsaking God for heathen confidences. <div eID="gen20690" type="x-p"/>
entries.36ee2f5b942b89504d061e04ca2cfbd5bdf79a0f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11432"/><div sID="gen20691" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11432"/><hi type="bold">14. vermilion--</hi>the peculiar color of the Chaldeans, as purple was of the Assyrians. In striking agreement with this verse is the fact that the Assyrian sculptures lately discovered have painted and colored bas-reliefs in red, blue, and black. The Jews (for instance Jehoiakim, <reference osisRef="Jer.22.14">Jr 22:14</reference>) copied these (compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.8.10">Eze 8:10</reference>). <div eID="gen20691" type="x-p"/>
entries.9ae08929bafa9a3375c28aa2b3be60fc8feff187: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11433"/><div sID="gen20692" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11433"/><hi type="bold">15. exceeding in dyed attire--</hi>rather, "in ample dyed turbans"; literally, "redundant with dyed turbans." The Assyrians delighted in ample, flowing, and richly colored tunics, scarfs, girdles, and head-dresses or turbans, varying in ornaments according to the rank.<div eID="gen20692" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20693" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Chaldea, ... land of their nativity--</hi>between the Black and Caspian Seas (see on <reference osisRef="Isa.23.13">Is 23:13</reference>).<div eID="gen20693" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20694" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">princes--</hi>literally, a first-rate military class that fought by threes in the chariots, one guiding the horses, the other two fighting. <div eID="gen20694" type="x-p"/>
entries.d6f0b3c9349ad851f1ec2a0f538c7143d660e4e2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11434"/><div sID="gen20695" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11434"/><hi type="bold">16. sent messengers ... into Chaldea--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.29">Eze 16:29</reference>). It was she that solicited the Chaldeans, not they her. Probably the occasion was when Judah sought to strengthen herself by a Chaldean alliance against a menaced attack by Egypt (compare 2Ki 23:29-35; 24:1-7). God made the object of their sinful desire the instrument of their punishment. Jehoiakim, probably by a stipulation of tribute, enlisted Nebuchadnezzar against Pharaoh, whose tributary he previously had been; failing to keep his stipulation, he brought on himself Nebuchadnezzar's vengeance. <div eID="gen20695" type="x-p"/>
entries.95f9ded6557c49c44cd4682ecc5696e62edadb3f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11435"/><div sID="gen20696" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11435"/><hi type="bold">17. alienated from them--</hi>namely, from the Chaldeans: turning again to the Egyptians (<reference osisRef="Ezek.23.19">Eze 23:19</reference>), trying by their help to throw off her solemn engagements to Babylon (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.37.5">Jr 37:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.37.7">7</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.7">2Ki 24:7</reference>). <div eID="gen20696" type="x-p"/>
entries.9f7fc8ebd60e5a6aa4f3910e1e2fae6a547a2949: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11436"/><div sID="gen20697" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11436"/><hi type="bold">18. my mind was alienated from her--</hi>literally, "was broken off from her." Just retribution for "her mind being alienated (broken off) from the Chaldeans" (<reference osisRef="Ezek.23.17">Eze 23:17</reference>), to whom she had sworn fealty (<reference osisRef="Ezek.17.12-Ezek.17.19">Eze 17:12-19</reference>). "Discovered" implies the open shamelessness of her apostasy. <div eID="gen20697" type="x-p"/>
entries.7100a79e4fccec69ccf088a172a2063071f8e1a2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11437"/><div sID="gen20698" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11437"/>19. Israel first "called" her lusts, practised when in Egypt, "to her (fond) remembrance," and then actually returned to them. Mark the danger of suffering the memory to dwell on the pleasure felt in past sins. <div eID="gen20698" type="x-p"/>
entries.e903f4decd5de0efb667233ad3a4e25001f0ec08: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11438"/><div sID="gen20699" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11438"/><hi type="bold">20. their paramours--</hi>that is, her paramours among them (the Egyptians); she doted upon their persons as her paramours (<reference osisRef="Ezek.23.5">Eze 23:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.12.16">12, 16</reference>).<div eID="gen20699" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20700" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">flesh--</hi>the membrum virile (very large in the ass). Compare <reference osisRef="Lev.15.2">Le 15:2</reference>, Margin; <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.26">Eze 16:26</reference>.<div eID="gen20700" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20701" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">issue of horses--</hi>the seminal issue. The horse was made by the Egyptians the hieroglyphic for a lustful person. <div eID="gen20701" type="x-p"/>
entries.740486354a183996a3170e08161cc2faf8913528: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11439"/><div sID="gen20702" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11439"/><hi type="bold">21. calledst to remembrance--</hi>"didst repeat" [Maurer].<div eID="gen20702" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20703" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in bruising--</hi>in suffering ... to be bruised. <div eID="gen20703" type="x-p"/>
entries.3a5039ba70f35cece98c28bbed46b216e8d5a8dc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11440"/><div sID="gen20704" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11440"/><hi type="bold">22. lovers ... alienated--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ezek.23.17">Eze 23:17</reference>). Illicit love, soon or late, ends in open hatred (<reference osisRef="2Sam.13.15">2Sa 13:15</reference>). The Babylonians, the objects formerly of their God-forgetting love, but now, with characteristic fickleness, objects of their hatred, shall be made by God the instruments of their punishment. <div eID="gen20704" type="x-p"/>
entries.7d532e30082cf131d68a70c5ac0ab6629dd86a1f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11441"/><div sID="gen20705" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11441"/><hi type="bold">23. Pekod, &c.--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.50.21">Jr 50:21</reference>). Not a geographical name, but descriptive of Babylon. "Visitation," peculiarly the land of "judgment"; in a double sense: actively, the inflicter of judgment on Judah; passively, as about to be afterwards herself the object of judgment.<div eID="gen20705" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20706" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Shoa ... Koa--</hi>"rich ... noble"; descriptive of Babylon in her prosperity, having all the world's wealth and dignity at her disposal. Maurer suggests that, as descriptive appellatives are subjoined to the proper name, "all the Assyrians" in the second hemistich of the verse (as the verse ought to be divided at "Koa"), so Pekod, Shoa, and Koa must be appellatives descriptive of "The Babylonians and ... Chaldeans" in the first hemistich; "Pekod" meaning "prefects"; Shoa ... Koa, "rich ... princely."<div eID="gen20706" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20707" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">desirable young men--</hi>strong irony. Alluding to <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.12">Eze 23:12</reference>, these "desirable young men" whom thou didst so "dote upon" for their manly vigor of appearance, shall by that very vigor be the better able to chastise thee. <div eID="gen20707" type="x-p"/>
entries.7d1d07a750139f994afbcc4785acfdab3930ac37: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11442"/><div sID="gen20708" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11442"/><hi type="bold">24. with chariots--</hi>or, "with armaments"; so the Septuagint; "axes" [Maurer]; or, joining it with "wagons," translate, "with scythe-armed wagons," or "chariots" [Grotius].<div eID="gen20708" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20709" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wheels--</hi>The unusual height of these increased their formidable appearance (<reference osisRef="Ezek.1.16-Ezek.1.20">Eze 1:16-20</reference>).<div eID="gen20709" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20710" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">their judgments--</hi>which awarded barbarously severe punishments (<reference osisRef="Jer.52.9">Jr 52:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.29.22">29:22</reference>). <div eID="gen20710" type="x-p"/>
entries.962571ea08fb327f1f1b1ea23e070fdf238850d1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11443"/><div sID="gen20711" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11443"/><hi type="bold">25. take away thy nose ... ears--</hi>Adulteresses were punished so among the Egyptians and Chaldeans.
